title: Prompt injection containment, direct and indirect
status_rationale: Unbound requires treating documents, messages, retrieved content and tool results as untrusted (AIN-012), removing prohibited tools in the broker rather than relying on prompts (UNB-AGT-003), keeping deterministic findings in a section AI cannot edit (CNV-AIO-002) and ensuring prompt injection cannot bypass deterministic financial or authorization controls (UNB-AIO-003). None is implemented. No equivalent rule was located for Echelon's own engineering agents.
target_answer: Echelon assumes prompt injection will sometimes succeed and limits what a successful injection can do. Product agents hold only A0 to A2 authority, every tool call is authorized by deterministic code against the principal's recorded authority (CNV-AIO-001), tools that can send data outside the tenant are removed by the broker for tasks that read untrusted content, and AI narrative cannot change or reorder deterministic findings shown to approvers. Uploaded documents are parsed into typed data at the Limen and Strata boundaries and passed to models as quoted data. Classifiers and prompt hardening are secondary layers measured in the adversarial suite. Engineering agents that read untrusted repositories, issues or web pages run with no production credentials and their changes pass human-controlled review and release gates.
current_practice: Not established for any production service. Engineering agent practices are unknown beyond the existence of human-reviewed pull request workflows described in repository governance documents.
intended_practice: Implement the tool broker and authority matrix first; then add the adversarial suite required by RR-AIN-027-r1.
customer_statement: Echelon's design contains prompt injection by architecture: AI components cannot execute consequential actions, cannot alter deterministic findings and receive untrusted content only as data. This design is not yet implemented or tested.
owner: Not assigned (proposed: Unbound platform security owner, with Tutela as security engineering discipline)
residual_risks: Injection can still distort AI narrative that a human reads, creating automation bias.
Read-only agents can still leak data they can read if any egress channel remains.

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want assurance that malicious content cannot hijack AI to leak data or take unauthorized actions.
challenge.adverse_outcome: An uploaded grant document instructs an assistant to change a payee or reveal another donor's data, and it does.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Input filters, injection classifiers and system prompt hardening reduce but do not eliminate injection; published research and the OWASP LLM Top 10 treat complete prevention as unsolved.
challenge.legally_required: Not specifically required by law; general security duties under GLBA safeguards and contracts apply.
challenge.contractually_required: Customers increasingly ask for named defenses (filters, guardrail products).
challenge.historical_convention: Borrowed from web application firewall thinking.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Within scope, consequential actions are eliminated from agent reach: there is no tool through which an injected instruction can approve, pay or change authority, and deterministic findings are hashed outside AI control.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Tool broker and API authorization enforce on every call.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Denial logs and adversarial suite results on every release.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Blast-radius limitation by authority and tool removal, with filters as secondary measured layers.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Verifiable by negative tests (AUTH-T01 style) and by inspecting the broker's tool sets per task.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely among security reviewers; procurement checklists may still ask for a named guardrail product.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If agents are later granted A3 actions or egress tools while reading untrusted content, the argument fails.
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-restriction may reduce AI usefulness and push users to unsanctioned tools.
supporting_arguments: Does not depend on winning an arms race against injection phrasing.
opposing_arguments: Read access alone can leak data if any output channel exists.
Humans may still act on injected narrative.

title: Tenant isolation of AI context, retrieval, caching and memory
status_rationale: Unbound requires agents to use the same governed APIs and tenant-scoped authorization as humans (UNB-AI-STD-001), a schema and database role per sponsor tenant with row-level security (CNV-ARC-001) and threat-tested partner isolation (CNV-ARC-002, AUTH-T05). AI-specific stores (embeddings, caches, memory) are not specified. Nothing is implemented.
target_answer: AI context is assembled only through tenant-scoped APIs under the requesting principal's authority, never from shared stores. Any embedding index, prompt cache, conversation memory or evaluation set is partitioned per tenant and keyed by tenant identity, and retrieval re-checks authorization at query time. Provider-side prompt caching is used only where cache scope is per account and Echelon's account structure prevents cross-tenant reuse. Engineering and operations agents have no standing access to production tenant data. Cross-tenant leakage tests run in CI with canary records.
intended_practice: Extend CNV-ARC-001 tenant partitioning to every AI store and add canary-based leakage tests to the isolation test suite.
customer_statement: Echelon's design requires AI features to use the same tenant-scoped authorization as human users and to keep any AI stores partitioned per customer. This is not yet implemented or tested.
owner: Not assigned (proposed: Unbound platform security owner)
residual_risks: Aggregate or benchmark features that intentionally span tenants (CNV-ECO-001) need separate privacy review.

title: Tool misuse and excessive agency
status_rationale: Unbound requires a capability manifest per agent (AIN-002), broker removal of prohibited tools (UNB-AGT-003), governed F# APIs instead of direct database writes (GOV-AUTH-023), and budgets for tokens, tools and time (RR-AIN-028-r1). Not implemented.
target_answer: Each agent task receives the smallest tool set needed, expressed as typed F# commands with validated parameters. Tools execute through the same server-side authorization as human calls, under the principal's identity, never a privileged service identity. Parameters that change money, recipients or authority are not agent-settable at all. Tools with external egress (email, web requests, rendering of remote URLs) are unavailable to tasks that process untrusted content. Every run has token, tool-call, time and cost budgets and stops safely when they are exhausted.
intended_practice: Implement per CNV-GOV-010 authority matrix and RR-AIN-028-r1 budgets.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to give each AI agent only the minimum typed tools for its task, authorized like a human request, with no ability to set amounts, recipients or permissions, and with enforced usage budgets. Not yet implemented.

title: Handling of model output as untrusted
status_rationale: The Secure Construction Standard (proposed) prohibits user-supplied HTML (SEC-UI-001), application JavaScript outside Limen (SEC-UI-002) and arbitrary evaluation (SEC-EXEC-001). Unbound requires AI outputs to be typed as Proposal, Finding or Explanation (RR-UNB-AI-STD-003-r1) and labeled (AIN-005). Limen exists as a library; none is operated in a production service.
target_answer: Model output is untrusted input. It is parsed into typed values or rendered as plain text with contextual encoding; it is never executed as code, SQL, shell or HTML, and remote resources it references are not fetched or rendered automatically. Outputs carry a type (Proposal, Finding, Explanation) and a label so they cannot be stored or displayed as authoritative records. Factual claims in AI narrative must cite stored evidence; uncited claims are marked as unverified.
current_practice: Not established for AI output. Limen (browser boundary library) and the proposed SEC-UI rules exist as design artifacts.
intended_practice: Apply SEC-UI-001, SEC-UI-002 and SEC-EXEC-001 to all AI output paths and implement typed AI output per RR-UNB-AI-STD-003-r1.
provable: Limen exists as a library that passes only serializable data across the browser boundary; it is not operated for an Echelon production service.
customer_statement: Echelon's design treats AI output as untrusted data: it is never executed, rendered as HTML or stored as an authoritative record. Echelon's Limen browser boundary library supports this, but it is not yet operated in a production service.
residual_risks: Plain-text misinformation can still mislead readers; labeling mitigates but does not remove it.

title: AI supply chain: models, AI libraries, agent frameworks, tool servers and data
status_rationale: SEC-SUPPLY-001 (proposed) requires approved, locked, provenance-checked dependencies with SBOM, and CNV-GOV-009 requires license checks in the SBOM, but neither addresses models, tool servers or AI datasets. Engineering agents' tool integrations and credentials are not inventoried in any record located.
target_answer: Models, AI SDKs, agent frameworks, tool servers and datasets are dependencies under SEC-SUPPLY-001: approved, pinned, provenance-verified and listed in the SBOM with AI-specific fields (model identifier, provider, version, dataset lineage). Third-party tool servers connected to any agent are approved per server and per tool, run with scoped credentials, and are re-reviewed on version change. Retrieval corpora and evaluation sets have recorded lineage and write access limited to deterministic ingestion jobs. Agent credentials are short-lived, scoped and never present in prompts or agent-readable files.
intended_practice: Extend SEC-SUPPLY-001 and the SBOM process to AI components and add a tool server approval list.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet extended its supply-chain controls to AI models, AI libraries and agent tool integrations. It plans to treat them as approved, pinned dependencies listed in its SBOM.
open_questions: Which tool integrations and credentials do Echelon's engineering agents currently have?

title: AI threat modeling against OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS, and production abuse monitoring
status_rationale: Tutela is Echelon's security engineering discipline for assets, trust boundaries, threats and controls; no AI threat model has been produced with it for any service. SOC2-012 requires monitoring of agent activity. Not implemented.
target_answer: Each AI feature has a Tutela threat model that records, for every OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 item and each applicable MITRE ATLAS technique, whether it applies, the control that addresses it and the test that proves it. Production monitoring alerts on authority-denial spikes, unusual tool sequences, injection markers in inputs, budget exhaustion and missing agent traces (AIN-033).
intended_practice: Produce threat models with Tutela as AI features are designed.
provable: Tutela exists as a discipline and repository; no AI threat model output exists for an Echelon service.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to threat-model every AI feature against the OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS and to monitor AI activity in production. No threat model or monitoring exists yet.

title: AI red teaming and adversarial testing
status_rationale: RR-AIN-027-r1 requires every model, prompt, tool or policy change to pass a frozen evaluation set and adversarial prompt-injection and authority-escalation suite in CI; GOV-AUTH-018 requires adversarial tests before autonomous consequential actions. No suite exists and no external AI red team or penetration test has occurred.
target_answer: An adversarial suite (direct and indirect injection, authority escalation, cross-tenant extraction, tool misuse, output-handling attacks) runs in CI and blocks release on failure. The suite grows from incidents, external research and external testing findings. Independent AI red teaming is performed before first production AI release and annually or on major change, and AI features are in scope of external penetration tests. Findings are tracked to retest.
current_practice: Not established. No external testing of any kind has occurred.
intended_practice: Build the CI suite first; commission independent testing before production.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet performed AI red teaming or external testing. It plans a release-blocking adversarial test suite in CI and independent AI red teaming before production use.

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want evidence that someone has tried hard to break the AI before attackers do.
challenge.adverse_outcome: A practical jailbreak or injection is found in production by an attacker.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: A periodic external AI red team finds issues at a point in time; results depend heavily on tester skill and scope and do not cover later changes.
challenge.legally_required: Not legally required for Echelon; EU AI Act requires adversarial testing for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which Echelon does not provide.
challenge.contractually_required: Increasingly requested in enterprise AI questionnaires.
challenge.historical_convention: Extends annual penetration test convention to AI.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Authority limits remove the highest-consequence outcomes regardless of test coverage.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: CI adversarial suite on every change.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Per-release suite results with corpus version.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Continuous release-blocking adversarial suite plus authority limits, with periodic independent red teaming as calibration rather than as the primary control.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Suite corpus, results and coverage are inspectable; independent testers can extend the corpus.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Likely if combined with at least one independent red team; unlikely if offered as a substitute for any independent test.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If the suite corpus is narrow or stale, continuous testing gives false confidence.
challenge.alternative_risks: Self-authored suites share the authors' blind spots, which matter more when AI agents author both code and tests.
supporting_arguments: Covers every change instead of one snapshot.
opposing_arguments: First-party only; independence is the point of red teaming.
Agent-written tests may encode the same assumptions as agent-written code.

title: Security of AI-generated code in Echelon's own software
status_rationale: Echelon builds its software largely with AI coding agents (Praxis provenance and agent instruction files in its repositories show this). The proposed Secure Construction Standard narrows weakness classes by construction (F# default, no dynamic SQL, no user HTML, no JavaScript outside Limen, no dynamic code), and Praxis records agent provenance; but the review, testing and scanning practices actually applied to AI-written code have not been documented, measured or independently verified. Strata has no verified runtime typed query interface, so SEC-DB-001 depends on a capability not found. Unbound requires two approvers on control-relevant modules (CNV-PLT-010), not yet operating.
target_answer: Echelon states openly that most code is written by AI coding agents and shows why that is acceptable: (1) language and architecture remove whole weakness classes regardless of author (memory-unsafe code, dynamic SQL, HTML injection sinks, arbitrary evaluation); (2) every change, whoever writes it, passes the same release gates: compiler with warnings as errors, property and negative tests, SAST, SCA with dependency allow-listing that defeats hallucinated or typosquatted packages, secret scanning; (3) changes to control-relevant modules need review by a human who did not prompt the change (CNV-PLT-010); (4) agents cannot weaken tests or gates, because changes to tests, gate configuration and security rules are themselves control-relevant; (5) Praxis records which agent, model and run produced each change, so defects can be traced to their source; (6) defect and vulnerability rates of agent-written code are measured and published to customers.
current_practice: AI coding agents are used. Review, test and scanning practice for their output is not documented in any record located; the Standard is proposed, not adopted.
intended_practice: Adopt the Secure Construction Standard, apply CNV-PLT-010 style dual review to Echelon's own control-relevant code, add dependency allow-listing and protected test and gate paths, and measure outcomes with Dokimos.
provable: Praxis provenance records agent contributions in repositories that use it. Nothing proves review or security analysis effectiveness for AI-written code.
customer_statement: Echelon develops its software largely with AI coding agents. Its proposed construction standard removes several vulnerability classes by language and architecture, and its tooling records which agent produced each change. Review, testing and scanning controls for AI-written code are not yet formally established or evidenced; Echelon plans to apply the same release gates to all code and human review to control-relevant changes.
residual_risks: Agents writing both code and tests can share blind spots; human review of control-relevant code is the compensating control.
Logic and authorization flaws are not removed by language choice.
open_questions: What proportion of merged changes across Echelon repositories are agent-authored, by agent and model?
Is any human review currently required before merge in Echelon repositories?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want to know whether AI-written software is as safe as human-written software and who is accountable for it.
challenge.adverse_outcome: An AI agent introduces an injection flaw, a backdoored or hallucinated dependency, or weakens an authorization check, and it ships.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: The conventional answer is human code review of every line. Research and practice show human review misses many vulnerabilities, and its effectiveness drops as volume rises, which is exactly what AI coding increases.
challenge.legally_required: No law prohibits AI-written code. NIST SP 800-218A sets expectations for AI model development, not for using AI to write code; customers' secure development expectations still apply.
challenge.contractually_required: Some customers now ask for disclosure of AI coding use; few contractually restrict it.
challenge.historical_convention: Assumes a human author who understands every line.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Language and architecture remove weakness classes for any author: memory safety, no dynamic SQL, no HTML injection sinks, no dynamic code. Dependency allow-listing removes hallucinated package risk.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Compiler, analyzers, tests and gates run on every change regardless of author.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Per-change provenance and gate results; measured defect rates by author type.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Construction-level elimination plus uniform automated gates plus targeted human review of control-relevant code, with provenance and measured outcomes, instead of claiming line-by-line human review of everything.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Verifiable by inspecting gate configuration, protected-path rules, provenance records and published defect metrics.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Uncertain; some bank and insurer reviewers will want human review of all production code regardless of evidence.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If gates are not actually enforced, or the Standard's assumptions fail (for example Strata cannot provide typed queries), elimination claims do not hold.
challenge.conventional_cost: high (human review of all AI-generated volume)
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-reliance on gates authored or maintained by the same agents.
supporting_arguments: Provenance makes accountability more precise than for typical human teams.
opposing_arguments: Logic flaws and business-rule errors are not caught by language choice.
Buyers may perceive AI authorship as higher risk regardless of controls.
Gate effectiveness is unproven until measured and externally tested.
